what_it_does: Modern server software (databases, web servers, cloud services) has enormous amounts of executable code, so the last-level cache — a large, slow on-chip storage area shared by all processor cores that acts as a buffer between the cores and main memory — gets hammered by instruction fetches rather than data. Sophisticated cache-replacement policies (algorithms that decide which stored item to evict when space runs out) designed for mixed workloads add complex hardware yet provide barely any benefit over simpler rules for these instruction-heavy patterns, especially when a prefetcher (hardware that pre-loads data it predicts will be needed soon) is also running. This paper proposes PACIPV, which stands for Prefetch-Aware Coarse-grained Insertion and Promotion Vectors. Rather than inventing a new rule by hand, it takes a well-known eviction framework called RRIP (Re-Reference Interval Prediction, which ranks each cache line by how soon it is likely to be needed again) and makes two knobs configurable: where in the priority ranking a newly loaded line is placed, and how much it is promoted after being used. The best combination of knobs is found by exhaustively testing all possibilities on representative workloads. The result distinguishes between lines fetched by the prefetcher versus lines fetched on demand, and the hardware is simple enough to add negligible chip area.
